name: Closed Spinal Dysraphism

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiological Diagnostic Criteria for Closed Spinal Dysraphism

criteria.description: Presence of cutaneous stigmata over the lumbosacral region such as dimples, tufts of hair, hemangiomas, or subcutaneous masses
MRI evidence of spinal cord or vertebral anomalies consistent with closed spinal dysraphism (e.g., tethered cord, lipoma, dermal sinus tract)
Neurological signs or symptoms attributable to spinal cord dysfunction such as lower limb weakness or bladder dysfunction

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: MRI evidence of spinal cord or vertebral anomalies consistent with closed spinal dysraphism is required; presence of cutaneous markers or neurological deficits supports diagnosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis often requires correlation of clinical findings with imaging studies; some cases may be asymptomatic and detected incidentally.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Cutaneous lumbosacral dimple with underlying spinal anomaly
searchTerms: skin dimple over lower spine with spinal defect
small skin pit on lower back with underlying spine issue

pathognomonic.notes: Neurological dysfunction due to abnormal spinal cord fixation

common.notes: Variable degrees of muscle weakness in legs

common.symptomName: Cutaneous hairy patch (hypertrichosis) over lumbosacral area
common.notes: Tuft of hair overlying spinal defect
searchTerms: hairy patch on lower back skin
skin area with abnormal hair growth on lower back

common.notes: Fatty mass associated with spinal dysraphism
searchTerms: fatty lump under skin in lower back
soft tissue fatty mass on lower back

occasional.notes: Epithelium-lined tract connecting skin to spinal canal
searchTerms: skin tract connecting surface to deeper tissues

occasional.notes: Numbness or altered sensation in legs
searchTerms: loss of feeling in lower limbs

occasional.symptomName: Orthopedic deformities such as foot deformities
Back pain localized to lumbosacral region

rare.notes: Spinal curvature secondary to cord tethering

searchTerms: increased muscle tone in lower limbs

imaging: MRI demonstrating tethered cord, lipoma, dermal sinus tract, or other spinal cord anomalies
Ultrasound in infants showing spinal cord abnormalities
genetic: No specific genetic mutation identified; multifactorial etiology suspected
other: Neurological examination revealing lower limb deficits

distinguishingFeatures: Open neural tube defect with exposed neural tissue
More severe neurological deficits at birth
Visible spinal defect without skin coverage
Can be secondary to closed spinal dysraphism but may occur independently

redFlags: Progressive lower limb weakness or paralysis
New onset or worsening bladder/bowel dysfunction
Rapidly enlarging subcutaneous mass or signs of infection over spinal lesion
references: Kumar R, et al. Closed spinal dysraphism: clinical and imaging features. Radiographics. 2019.
Tethered Cord Syndrome and Occult Spinal Dysraphism. J Neurosurg Pediatr. 2020.
